item.title: Michael Nielsen removes his neural networks book citing accelerated AI risks and ethical concerns [ ! ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Michael Nielsen has taken down his book on neural networks and deep learning, expressing concern over the rapid advancement of AI systems by frontier labs and the insufficient time humanity has to address associated risks. He believes these developments pose significant catastrophic risks and that continuing to educate people in this area could contribute to the problem. Nielsen outlines his view that the fundamental threat is not just loss of control to AI but the emergence of easily developed, catastrophic technologies enabled by advanced AI, which outpace social and institutional defenses. He argues that addressing AI safety requires broader societal solutions beyond technical alignment of individual systems, emphasizing the need for global safety measures to manage the destructive potential latent in nature.

item.title: Google introduces DeepCrossAttention to improve transformer residual connections, achieving comparable model quality up to three times faster with minimal parameter increase [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Google Research has developed DeepCrossAttention (DCA), a new transformer architecture that enhances residual connections by dynamically combining outputs from previous layers using learnable weights and depth-wise cross-attention. This approach addresses the information dilution problem in traditional residual connections, enabling models to train up to three times faster while maintaining or improving quality with only a slight increase in parameters. DCA replaces the standard point-wise summation in residual connections with dynamic routing that allows each layer to selectively retrieve features from earlier layers on a per-token basis. Experiments on language modeling and image classification benchmarks demonstrated that DCA improves convergence speed, training stability, and final model performance compared to standard transformers and alternative connection methods.

item.title: Researchers find frontier AI models can identify human or AI authorship from a single text, often pinpointing specific labs or individuals [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: A new study shows that advanced AI models like Claude Fable 5.2, GPT-6.1 Sol, and Gemini 4 Carbon can determine whether a text was written by a human or AI with a simple zero-shot prompt. These models can also identify the AI lab responsible or, in many cases, the exact human author, achieving high accuracy on datasets including anonymous ICML 2020 reviews and prolific Reddit users. The ability depends on the model's exposure to the author's writing during pretraining and the reasoning effort applied. This capability poses significant challenges to anonymity for individuals with substantial online writing, with limited options for defense.

item.title: China's entertainment industry shifts as AI generates over 90% of new micro dramas in 2026, displacing many live actors [ * ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: In 2026, more than 90% of China's new micro dramas were produced using AI, including actors, voices, and scenes, leading to significant job losses for traditional actors like Oksana. These AI-generated short dramas, often fantasy or romantic-themed and designed for mobile viewing, have become highly popular, with some series drawing billions of views. The shift to AI production has drastically reduced costs and manpower, allowing small teams to create content that previously required large crews and sets. Despite the volume of AI micro dramas produced, only a small fraction achieve significant viewership or profitability. The Chinese government supports the development of AI-driven cultural content as part of its broader AI adoption goals, though many former actors have turned to other work amid the industry's transformation. While AI micro dramas dominate short-form content, some industry insiders believe that live human acting will remain essential for longer-form productions due to AI's limitations in conveying subtle emotions and imperfections.

item.title: Google adds official Google AI plan support to Pi coding agent with Gemini model access via Interactions API [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Google has integrated official support for its AI plans into the Pi coding agent, enabling users to sign in with Google OAuth and access Gemini models through the Interactions API. This update includes features like streaming, tool calls, usage tracking, and error handling for plan limits and eligibility. The integration uses a secure OAuth flow with PKCE and DPoP-bound refresh tokens, and the default model is gemini-4-hydrogen. This enhancement allows third-party apps like Pi and Hermes Agent to run Gemini models on a user's Google AI plan quota, improving the agent's capabilities and user experience.

item.title: OpenAI claims to have solved a 57-year-old matrix multiplication exponent problem, establishing a lower bound of 2.25 for square matrix multiplication [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: OpenAI announced a claimed solution to a longstanding mathematical problem in theoretical computer science related to the exponent of square matrix multiplication, a challenge dating back to 1969. Their preprint presents a lower bound matching their previously reported upper bound of 2.25, potentially defining the mathematical limit for this computation central to AI and numerical libraries. The company released nine manuscripts applying a new geometric theory of tensors to arithmetic complexity and combinatorics, with independent researchers from LMU Munich confirming similar upper bounds using alternative methods. OpenAI also provided a Lean formalization of their proof, though some aspects remain unformalized. This breakthrough could guide future AI infrastructure development by clarifying performance limits in matrix multiplication algorithms.

The discussion also touches on concerns related to Anthropic, potential loss of control, and the concept of AI handoverism.

item.title: Experts warn AI labs may be withholding breakthroughs in cryptography that could disrupt global encryption security soon [ ! ] [ ⬢ ]
item.description: Experts including theoretical computer scientists and mathematicians warn that leading AI labs might have made significant advances in solving longstanding mathematical problems underlying encryption used by banks, governments, and spy agencies. These breakthroughs could enable rapid decryption of sensitive communications, potentially forcing a sudden overhaul of global security protocols. The concerns arise from recent AI-driven mathematical results suggesting AI's capability to tackle problems once thought unsolvable in the near term. While no official disclosures have been made, experts believe these findings could either reveal new methods to break encryption or confirm its robustness, with major implications for digital security. Governments and financial institutions have been preparing for quantum computing threats over the next decade, but AI advances may accelerate this timeline unexpectedly. Authorities and industry leaders are urging caution and transparency as the potential impact of these AI discoveries remains uncertain. The situation underscores the urgency for accelerated development and deployment of next-generation encryption standards to safeguard electronic secrets against emerging AI capabilities.

item.title: NVIDIA and Kioxia test 1.1PB NVMe SSD memory system across 18 nodes, enabling GPU addressable petabyte-scale storage for AI workloads [ * ] [ ⬢ ]
item.description: NVIDIA and Kioxia conducted an experiment in November 2026 using an 18-node cluster equipped with 60TB NVMe SSDs per node, achieving a total of 1.1 petabytes of addressable memory. This system integrates SSD storage directly into the GPU memory address space, extending traditional memory hierarchies by combining high-bandwidth memory speed with large SSD capacity. The architecture builds on NVIDIA's Storage-Next initiative and aims to blur the lines between fast memory and storage, potentially benefiting large-scale AI applications such as vector databases and retrieval-augmented generation pipelines. While not primarily designed for larger single-node language models yet, this approach could enable latency-sensitive access to massive embedded data volumes, representing a significant shift in AI infrastructure design.

item.title: GitHub integrates AI agents into Dependabot to improve dependency management and automate major version upgrades [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: GitHub is enhancing Dependabot by incorporating AI agents to address limitations in current dependency update tools. The new system, exemplified by the Felix project, automates coherent version bumps across multiple files, reads release notes, applies necessary code migrations, and verifies builds before opening pull requests, aiming to reduce manual maintenance and improve security. Traditional update bots like Dependabot and Renovate often leave fragmented upgrades and require manual intervention for major version changes, leading to merge conflicts and outdated dependencies. Felix uses AI to group related updates, handle major version migrations automatically, and ensure consistency across toolchains and configuration files, running tests in sandbox environments to verify changes before proposing them. This approach aims to alleviate "dependency burnout" by reducing the manual effort needed to keep software dependencies current and secure, potentially improving developer productivity and software reliability in environments with frequent updates and security vulnerabilities.

item.title: Ivankahl.com explains how to safely use asynchronous AI agents to automate coding tasks with pre-planning and review workflows [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: The article outlines the challenges and necessary practices for enabling AI agents to work autonomously on software development tasks without continuous human supervision. It emphasizes the importance of clear specifications, secure environments, automated checks, and human review at key points to ensure quality and safety when delegating work to asynchronous AI agents. It describes how asynchronous agentic development differs from synchronous interaction by shifting control from real-time oversight to upfront planning and post-task review. The article also discusses risks such as security vulnerabilities and faulty code, recommending automated enforcement of rules and sandboxed execution to mitigate these issues. It advises against using asynchronous agents for exploratory or poorly specified tasks, highlighting the need for human feedback in such cases.

Labs sometimes pay premiums for exclusive data that competitors cannot access, highlighting the competitive nature of the coding data market.

item.title: OpenAI's GPT-6.2 Astra autonomously identifies creator of an anonymous 1808 sketchbook using public and archival sources in under 30 minutes [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: OpenAI's latest model, GPT-6.2 Astra, demonstrated the ability to conduct autonomous historical research by identifying the creator of an anonymous 1808 sketchbook held at Yale's Beinecke Library. The model quickly analyzed publicly available primary and secondary sources, including a previously overlooked paper archive, to form and verify a hypothesis, achieving a significant discovery in Canadian and fur trade history. Tested in late 2026, GPT-6.2 Astra showed strong capabilities in handling complex, open-ended tasks over extended periods, outperforming earlier models in accuracy and thoroughness. Despite occasional unusual communication styles, its underlying research and conclusions were reliable, suggesting advancements in AI's ability to tackle non-deterministic domains like history beyond deterministic fields such as mathematics. This breakthrough indicates a growing potential for AI models to contribute meaningfully to historical scholarship by autonomously generating new insights from scattered and incomplete evidence, marking a notable step in the evolution of AI-assisted research.

item.title: Quanta AI launches AI chat for managing virtual machines in VirtualProg on macOS using Apple Intelligence [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Quanta AI is an AI chat tool integrated into VirtualProg that allows users to manage virtual machines on macOS by issuing natural language commands such as starting, suspending, or creating VMs. It operates using Apple Intelligence either on-device or via Apple's Private Cloud Compute, requiring no account or API key, and includes safeguards for destructive actions that require user confirmation. The interface includes a sidebar for saved chats, a chat window showing commands and results, and a VM status strip. It supports scheduling, network configuration, and device attachment commands, with passwords managed securely outside the chat. Quanta AI saves chat history locally and offers features like search, export, and automatic cleanup. When Private Cloud usage limits are reached or offline, it falls back to on-device processing. The tool is designed for clear, single-task interactions and can integrate with larger AI assistants for complex workflows.

item.title: The Information's 2026 Gift Guide
item.description: In a twisted version of future Christmases, perhaps AIs will carry out all the tasks involved in gift giving. But lucky for us, Andy Jassy still has all the bots blocked! So here once again is The Information's annual Gift Guide, a project that we pursue with as much consideration and rigor as our everyday reporting. None of these items come via a publicist's pitch, and none of the suggestions contain affiliate links. These are all things that we genuinely love and can picture wrapping up ourselves. Suffice it to say, there's nothing artificial about our studious consideration and good taste. Entertainment I couldn't afford most Nintendo 64 games growing up, so I was a frequent presence at the local video game rental store: I distinctly remember taking home the original version of "The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time"-and needing to return it jusstttt as I was on the cusp of saving Hyrule, the game's fictional realm, and beating the big baddie, Ganondorf. This Switch 2 remake of the game has given me a shot at redemption. It's one of the most critically lauded games of the year-and for good reason. The graphics are dazzling, and I can only describe them as "wet": Everyone looks magnificently dewy. I also cannot overrecommend the nostalgia dopamine hit from getting to rummage through those treasure chests again.-Justin McCraw, senior software engineer A couple of weeks ago, the internet was abuzz about an AI-generated trailer that imagined an alt-history in which Nazi Germany and America wage some sort of temporal war. Sure, the clip was cool, but I still have my doubts about whether we're yet at the point where AI can make a comprehensible feature film. In the meantime, there's "Fatherland," a 1992 alt-history bestseller from Robert Harris, the ultra-dependable thriller author. It imagines a 1960s landscape where Nazi Germany triumphed in Europe during World War II, and an aging Hitler clings to power. I think it's Harris' best world-building effort, which he accomplished through an enormous amount of research into how Hitler's chief architect, Albert Speer, hoped to transform Berlin. (Those plans included the Volkshalle, a massive dome; in the novel, Harris supersizes Speer's own ambitions, imagining the Volkshalle as a structure large enough to have its own microclimate.) "Fatherland" is taut as hell and completely unputdownable-with a weary, disillusioned city police captain, Xavier March, caught up in an intricate plot that runs through the Reich's highest ranks. As March investigates, he keeps practically tripping over dead bodies. Then there's the mystery of the terrible secrets kept in a hidden Swiss bank account.-Abram Brown, features editor

At one point I asked if they could fix things up if I had a stain on my shirt and they said absolutely not - they present photographs as they were taken, with cropping and balancing applied but no edits beyond that. The photo at the top of https://www.nytimes.com/2026/02/02/technology/moltbook-ai-so... is my laptop, taken in my garden, after hunting around for the best spot that didn't have too much glare on the screen. item.title: How Bankers Are Turning Tech Stock Volatility Into Cash [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Tech firms spending heavily on AI buildouts have flooded the market with new stock sales this year. And with investments in AI infrastructure soaking up so much investor cash, raising money for other capital-hungry areas of tech like quantum computing and robotics is requiring especially creative dealmaking. For companies that are already public but need more cash for ambitious projects, sharp swings in their share prices are making it tough to sell more stock at an attractive price. Bankers say one workaround is turning that volatility into a selling point by bundling shares with warrants, which give investors the right to buy more stock later at a locked-in price. If investors are willing to pay up for a chance at a future payoff, companies can sell stock at a premium rather than the usual discount for new share sales. One recent example is quantum computing company IonQ, which raised $2 billion in mid-October at a 15% premium to its prior closing price. In the IonQ deal, investors got stock plus warrants to buy more shares at double the stock's pre-offering price within the next seven years, an extra way for them to profit if IonQ's stock soars. IonQ has raised $5 billion in total through three such offerings since July 2025, helping pay for an acquisition spree that expanded its business into chip manufacturing and cybersecurity. The company's stock has been volatile over that period, falling sharply from an October 2025 high of $82, rebounding to about $70 this May and then tumbling again. The shares currently trade around $21. With tech investors particularly skittish right now, there's more reason for cash-hungry companies to pounce on any opportunities to raise money. That's also boosting the appeal of at-the-market stock sales, which allow companies to sell shares gradually into the open market, giving them the flexibility to take advantage of rallies. And while less conventional ways of raising equity were once viewed on Wall Street as signs of desperation, bankers say that stigma has faded in recent years as companies have embraced the benefits of having more options for raising cash. "Historically, ATMs and some of these more creative financing tools have been a bit of a scarlet letter...it was hard to get a management team or board around them," said Connor Leahey, managing director at Cohen & Co. Capital Markets. "And now it's totally shifted." But getting to the public market in the first place has also become much tougher. Investors have had to sop up a surge in new stock issued by already-public tech giants this year alongside mega listings from SpaceX and last week's debut by Anthropic, with most of those shares performing poorly after their IPOs. The broader market for tech debuts has all but dried up, and Anthropic's rapid drop below its offering price doesn't bode well for other IPO hopefuls. That helps explain a comparative burst of activity in mergers with special purpose acquisition companies. Five companies went public via a SPAC merger in October, including two space technology firms and a semiconductor tech company, according to data and analytics company Boardroom Alpha. Four more companies have gone public via SPAC so far this month, including robotics company Agility Robotics and spacecraft developer Quantum Space. Public debuts via SPAC boomed in 2020 and 2021 before falling sharply in recent years after a string of poorly performing deals and other market headwinds. But companies and bankers are taking a renewed look at SPACs as an IPO alternative. In a SPAC deal, a cash-poor private tech firm is acquired by a cashed-up public shell of a company. (SPAC stands for special purpose acquisition company). "SPACs are still alive," said Steven Halperin, co-head of capital solutions and head of public equity markets at Moelis & Co. "And as the IPO market gets more fickle and transaction sizes become larger and larger, will more companies think about going this route?" One reason why the SPAC route may be more appealing right now is a proposed regulatory change that could make it easier for newly public companies to raise new equity after their debut. One drawback of SPACs is that they don't guarantee a big infusion of cash, since investors in the SPAC can typically cash out their shares before the merger closes, which they often do if they don't like the business getting acquired. The Securities and Exchange Commission in May proposed easing restrictions on stock sales by newly public companies, including ones that go public via a SPAC. Among other changes, the proposal would eliminate a one-year waiting period for newly public companies to register for fast-tracked stock offerings. That could make it easier for those companies to take advantage of rallies in their share prices, including through ATMs and other deals already gaining traction with their public peers. item.title: AI Safety Advocates Sour on Anthropic [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Anthropic has built its brand in significant part around AI safety, presenting itself as a cautious foil to OpenAI. But the Claude developer has been losing loyalty lately from some safety advocates who say its rapid technological progress-sure to be aided by the funds raised in its blockbuster initial public offering last week-is increasing the chances that AI will run amok. While OpenAI has struggled with its own safety issues, it operates more like a normal tech startup, but "Anthropic seems more like a cult devoted to creating the machine gods as soon as possible or whatever, and that seems worse," said Ronny Fernandez, a longtime AI safety proponent who works at Lightcone Infrastructure, the organization that runs the online AI safety forum LessWrong. Criticism of Anthropic has grown louder in recent weeks as the company appears to be using its AI models to automate AI research, only a couple months after CEO Dario Amodei called on AI companies to "pace" the technology's development.

item.title: In Private Funding, Like IPOs, Big Companies Dominate [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Shares of Anthropic fell below its $83 IPO price on Tuesday morning, summing up what has been a tough year for IPOs. While a couple of monster IPOs got done-Anthropic and SpaceX-only a handful of others made it through including offerings from SK Hynix, Cerebras and Lime. And as of Tuesday, all of those were trading below their IPO price. That makes it the fifth year in a row when the IPO market has been at least a bit disappointing. A bunch of companies are lined up for next year-including OpenAI-but slumping tech valuations fueled by skepticism about the AI boom clouds prospects for 2027. In that context, it's a decent time to take the pulse of startup dealmaking. One thing is clear: as in the IPO market this year, in the private fundraising market, the biggest companies are dominating. The top 10 private companies have more than doubled their combined valuation from $1.1 trillion to $2.6 trillion in just one year, Goldman's top tech banker Jane Dunlevie said on stage last week at Goldman Sachs' annual private tech conference in Las Vegas. She was talking about OpenAI, Anthropic, Databricks, Stripe, Waymo, Revolut, Anduril, Ramp, Cognition and Jeff Bezos's Prometheus. And more than half of those-OpenAI, Databricks, Anduril, Stripe, Ramp and Cognition-are now trying to raise billions more. There's still plenty of smaller startups emerging. Goldman managed to play matchmaker for more than 400 investors and 400-plus startups in the gilded corridors at the Encore Wynn Hotel. The mood was still electric, though investors are starting to think: as public market valuations fall, how should we value these private companies? One reason why private valuations can stay elevated even as public stocks drop is that venture investors tend to zoom in on growth. Many of these AI businesses' revenues have taken off, even as they bleed money thanks to expensive AI models they run and the chips they need to buy or rent. At a fireside chat at last week's confab, Winston Weinberg, CEO of legal AI startup Harvey, acknowledged that even with fast revenue growth, its gross margins fell to about negative 55% around June. They improved the figure by about 95% in roughly three months. Weinberg said annualized revenue grew from $190 million at the end of last year and expected to end this year with at least $675 million. "We're still early in the build out of AI, which means many of the defining companies of this era are not yet public and many investors are just getting to see the potential of those companies, both on growth and margin." Goldman's Jane Dunlevie said in an interview on the sidelines. She said each tech era has its own tests with investors: for internet companies, it was a path to profit; for subscription software firms, it was predictable revenue and net revenue retention. Meanwhile, attendees at the conference were staying hopeful about next year's IPO market. Some predicted that older venture-backed startups, such as Vercel, Ramp and Plaid, and even the older vertical software companies with some AI makeover, such as AlphaSense and Clio, will finally go public. In the two days of investors' schmoozing over fancy desserts and cocktails, a lineup of popular AI, chip and cybersecurity startups, like Legora, Unconventional AI and Abnormal AI fielded dozens of investors' meeting requests. Many older software startups were trying to remind investors they still exist. They are not getting too much love, say bankers and investors. One barometer of who's important in Las Vegas this year was whom Goldman Sachs CEO David Solomon invited to his private dinner at the fancy restaurant Delilah. In attendance: Legora CEO Max Junestrand and Fireworks CEO Lin Qiao, said people familiar with the dinner. item.title: OpenAI Preps 'Athena' Data Tool to Make its Agents More Accurate [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: In its effort to win more business customers, OpenAI this fall launched an agent designed to help firms analyze their data and get answers to internal questions about their business. But at least one customer that has used the agent so far has found it isn't yet accurate enough for widespread use. That's a big problem. But OpenAI isn't sitting still. Representatives of the ChatGPT creator have told some customers and partners that they are developing a data management platform to help the agent perform better, according to the customer and three other people who spoke to OpenAI in recent weeks. The data management platform, code-named Athena, has similarities to what is known in the industry as a semantic layer, which companies use to create standardized definitions for business metrics such as revenue and customers, one of the people said. This type of software helps agents understand the difference between gross revenue and net revenue, or active and paying customers, the person added. One of the biggest reasons agents fail when companies use them with large amounts of complex business data is that they have to work out on their own what the data means and how it fits together, said Jason Strimpel, a managing director at Andersen Consulting who helps large companies use AI. "A semantic layer gives the agent that context from the start, often with plain-English descriptions of each item, so the agent has to guess less and [can work] faster and more accurately," he said.

item.title: Three LLM inflection points in twelve months [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: I gave a keynote at the AI Engineer Code Summit a couple of weeks ago, constructed around the idea that there have been three significant inflection points in the abilities of LLMs and coding agents in the past twelve months. Here's the video of the talk. In this post I'm going to pull out the major inflection point theme and interrogate it more deeply. Coding agents in November 2025 Today, November 24th 2026, is the one year anniversary of the release of Claude Opus 4.5. With hindsight, this was a consequential model. In the Opus 4.5 announcement, Anthropic said: Testers noted that Claude Opus 4.5 handles ambiguity and reasons about tradeoffs without hand-holding. They told us that, when pointed at a complex, multi-system bug, Opus 4.5 figures out the fix. They said that tasks that were near-impossible for Sonnet 4.5 just a few weeks ago are now within reach. This held up. Claude Code was 9 months old at that point, having been introduced alongside Claude 3.7 Sonnet on February 24th, 2025. Opus 4.5 was the first model I had used with Claude Code where the default result was generally the right thing. I hadn't been using Claude Code as a daily driver because it didn't feel reliable enough - I had to correct it often enough that it didn't feel like a clear accelerant. The new Opus changed that. For most of the coding problems I faced on a daily basis, Opus would get them right. It was clearly faster than working through the problems myself. Also in November, OpenAI released GPT-5.1 Instant, GPT-5.1 Thinking, GPT-5.1-Codex, and GPT-5.1-Codex-Max. These had a similar effect on their Codex coding agent: it became reliably useful for many of my coding tasks. The timing was convenient, because the December holidays were upon us. A lot of people, myself included, spent December tinkering with these new tools to see what they could do. By January we were ready to use them for our actual work. Fable class models in June/July We got our first hint of Claude Fable in April, when Anthropic announced Claude Mythos and said that it was too dangerous to release, due to its improved cybersecurity capabilities. Mythos was a model that could not just find security vulnerabilities, it could also figure out how to exploit them. In June we got to see how good that model was for ourselves, with the release of Claude Fable 5 - a defanged Mythos, that would solve most problems but would actively block you from using it for security work. After three glorious days... the US government took it away from us. Fable 5 was placed under export controls that effectively banned the model. We wouldn't get it back until July 1st. For me, Fable was an inflection point because it introduced us to what I now think of as Fable class models. My definition of these: In June I wrote about how Claude Fable is relentlessly proactive, after I asked it to help fix a display glitch in Safari and it spun up its own pyobjc-framework-Quartz screenshot mechanism and a CORS-enabled localhost logging server to help resolve the bug. A more recent example of the power of Fable class models is my mysterious beep finder from a couple of weeks ago. I gave Opus 5.5 and then Fable 5.2 access to five WebAudio microphones in a room full of boxes and it was able to triangulate the source of an infuriating mysterious beep to within about 40cm. Give it a goal, give it the right tools, and watch it cook. I'd currently class Claude Fable 5, 5.1, 5.2 and Claude Opus 5.5 as Fable class (I think of Opus 5.5 as "cheap Fable"). GPT-6 Astra got there for me too, and I think the new Gemini 4 Neon may count as well. These now represent the baseline for what I expect from a frontier model. 3D modeling and game development in September/October Something interesting happened with frontier LLMs over just the past four months: they got really good at 3D modeling. Set them up with Blender or ask them to write Three.js code and they'll produce credible models of almost anything you ask for. I first noticed this with Claude Fable 5, but it really kicked into gear with Opus 5.5, GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-6 Astra, and most recently the Gemini 4 family. Here's Gemini 4 Neon's attempt at "Make a three js animation where yonkers stands up as a big mech (cool stand up motion) and stomps around manhattan and queens and Brooklyn, use openstreetmap mapping data", for example. 3D spatial awareness is crucial if you want to use vision LLMs for robotics. I don't know if 3D modeling capabilities are a side-effect of the labs focusing on that or vice-versa. Back in August I experimented with having Fable 5 build me a raccoon heist game. It had 3D graphics, looked like a game, and played really poorly. GPT-5.6 Sol Ultra did a much better job but the game itself was still pretty dull after the first 90 seconds of play. I was somewhat relieved that designing a game that was fun appeared to remain a uniquely human pursuit. I even used that in a talk in September to reassure people that us humans still had a role to play! Then, I tried telling Claude Opus 5.5 "This game isn't fun enough yet. Make it a LOT more fun." And it worked. My Battledrones Command & Conquer-style RTS went from boring to deeply entertaining overnight, after Opus spent 12 hours playtesting new features and rebalancing the gameplay. Opus 5.5 was the first model I'd used that appeared to understand fun. I've since worked on several little game projects where prompts like "Think hard about how to make sure it is both fun and beautiful" produced results that kept me engaged for significant amounts of time. It's good at 3D modeling, too. Here's the "Goliath" mech from my Battledrones game, as seen in the model viewer debug tool: Opus 5.5 came out on September 22nd, 2026. I've been to two different conferences since then where people showed me game projects they'd been working on that really did feel like proper, worthwhile games. The indie games scene has descended into a full-blown culture war over AI-assisted programming. A lot of people are calling GTA VI the last pre-generative AI blockbuster. It feels like another inflection point to me. Is Fable 5.2 an inflection point too? I'm still trying to decide if Fable 5.2 represents a new inflection point, or just another incremental improvement. I'm getting so much done with that model right now! It seems to have taste that almost exactly matches my own. I have been burning through all sorts of gnarly problems that I've been thinking about (or procrastinating on) for several years now. The release notes for Datasette 1.0a42, 1.0a43, and 1.0a44 - plus LLM 0.37, 0.37.1, 0.37.2, 0.37.3, and 0.38 - all in the last three weeks, represent a flood of fixes, features and improvements. If this does represent an inflection point, the key feature seems to be that if you can imagine and then clearly describe a piece of software, Fable can build it. That's a wild thing to say, but it matches my experience over the past few weeks. Software development has transformed beyond recognition in the last year. I don't think I'll ever go back to typing most of my code by hand. Tags: game-design, my-talks, ai, generative-ai, llms, annotated-talks, coding-agents, claude-code, codex, claude-mythos-fable
